title: Tailplane Attachment Inspection Findings at First Heavy Check — Great Basin Airways
abstract: Great Basin Airways found fretting and coating breakdown at the tailplane attachment fittings during its first heavy checks, ahead of the interval the maintenance programme assumes, and asks for a standard that does not need repeat attention every check.

sections.request: Our first two aeroplanes through the heavy check both showed the same thing at the tailplane attachments: bright fretting marks on the mating faces and the protective coating gone in patches around two of the fitting bores. Nothing is cracked and nothing is out of limits, but our inspectors do not like it and neither do we, because it is early. Cleaning it up and recoating adds three shifts to a check that is already long. We are asking for a fitting arrangement that does not do this, or a proper standard for what we are supposed to accept and how often we have to look.
sections.background: Both aeroplanes are high utilisation, roughly eleven cycles a week, mostly short sectors on a long haul airframe. We have shared photographs and thickness readings with the field service representative. A third airframe due in the shop next spring will tell us whether this is fleet wide. Our shop has been recoating to the standard practice manual and that is holding, but it is not a fix.
sections.expected_outcome: Either a fitting standard that does not fret at this rate, or a written inspection and refurbishment interval we can plan into the check package instead of discovering it every time. We would like to know before our spring shop visit which of the two we are getting.

type_data.business_justification: Three additional shifts per heavy check on two aircraft already, projected across nine airframes over the next four years, with an unplanned refurbishment scope that the operator cannot quote to its lessor.
